course.title: Peritonitis
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Boundaries: diaphragm, posterior abdominal wall (spine and Quadratus lumborum), antero-lateral abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, oblique, transversus with their fascia and aponeurosis), diaphragm of the pelvis (Levator ani, coccigeus muscles)
  • Peritoneum = closed sack wrapped in thin membrane, which covers the internal surfaces of the abdomen (parietal peritoneum); the posterior parietal peritoneum reflects anterior and wraps most of abdominal organs (intraperitoneal organs, transverse mesocolon and mesentery) and becomes “ visceral peritoneum”)
  • Intraperitoneal organs: stomach, liver, gallbladder, first part of duodenum, pancreas (only tail), spleen, small bowel, appendix, transvers colon, sigmoid colon
  • Retroperitoneal space situated behind peritoneal cavity, between posterior parietal peritoneum and posterior muscular wall
  • Retroperitoneal organs: esophagus, aorta, vena cava, duodenum, pancreas (head and body), bladder, ureters, kidneys, adrenal glands, ascending and descending colon
  • Peritoneal organs have a serosa
  • Retroperitoneal organs have an adventitia

Definition

= inflammation (vascular congestion, edema) of visceral and parietal peritoneum, triggered by local, regional or general pathology

Classification 1

generalized
abscess

Classification 2

Primary/ secondary/ tertiary

Macroscopic

  • Peritoneal serosa, greater omentum and loops are hyperemic + exudate in peritoneal cavity
  • Sequestration of fluid in a true “third sector” → hypovolemia or hypovolemic shock
  • Accumulation of intraluminal fluid → hydroelectrolytic imbalance
  • Loops are distended and immobile = dynamic occlusion explained by Stoke’s law (inflammation of visceral

peritoneum causes paralysis of subjacent loop musculature)

  • Pneumococci pus is creamy, yellow and without smell
  • Pyocyanic bacillus (Pseudomonas) = nosocomial flora; greenish pus with specific aromatic odor
  • Serous fluid at opening of peritoneal cavity becomes opalescent and totally purulent at site of perforation

Presentation

  • extremely variable and depending on
    • Location
    • Time since its onset
    • Initial state of perforated organ
    • Biological state of patient
    • Possible treatments administered prior or during course of disease
Pain- Insidious onset, initially reduced and progressively increases
→ corresponds to visceral inflammation towards perforation
- Sudden appearance of violent, stabbing epigastric pain → perforated ulcer
- Location of pain usually corresponds to site of perforation
Vomiting- Is inconsistent
- Appears in advanced stages
- It increases hypovolemia
Transit
disorders		- Most frequently due to dynamic ileus
- Primitive peritonitis may have diarrheic onset
General
signs		= not constant
- Fever (38-39°C) may be absent
- Gonococcal peritonitis starts with 40°C fever
- Tachycardia (increases with fever; absence of this correlation is a sign for severity)
- Shock or persistent hypotension → renal failure
- Polypnea as a result of fever
- Tachypnea and superficial respiration due to meteorism and diaphragmatic irritation
Position- Pat. with peritonitis walk with their trunk flexed and hand on abdomen

Physical exam

Inspection- Immobile
- Superficial respiration
Palpation- Tenderness to palpation
- Increased abdominal wall rigidity = earliest, most reliable sign of peritonitis
- Voluntary and involuntary guarding
- Blumberg sign (not very specific)
- Cutaneous abdominal reflexes disappear and cutaneous hyperesthesia occurs = Dieulafoy’s sign
- Rectal or vaginal exam is painful and may evidence a fluctuant Douglas pouch
Percussion- Disappearance of prehepatic dullness → pneumoperitoneum due to perforations
- Bell or Grassmann-Mandel sign defines pain produced on percussion of peritonitis
Auscultation- Usually reveals abdominal silence, in accordance withStoke’s law

Lab/ imaging

  • Leukocytosis with left shift (neutrophilia)
    • Leukopenia is a sign of severity
  • Upright plain abdominal X-ray → pneumoperitoneum; fluid collection causes loss of psoas shadow; distension of loops with air-fluid levels secondary to dynamic ileus
    • Post-OP pneumoperitoneum persists for 3 days
  • Chest X-ray for exclusion of thoracic causes
  • US → intraperitoneal fluid collections; limited for gaseous loop distension
  • CT and MRI → diagnosis of collections (rarely used in emergency)
  • Lavage puncture (paracentesis) and diagnostic laparoscopy should be carefully used → injury risk
  • Laparoscopy has advantage of changing in favorable cases from diagnostic procedure into therapeutic gesture

Primary peritonitis (PP)

= spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)

  • 2 main characteristics
    • Mostly monomicrobial (>90%) !!!
    • Low level of proteins and leucocytes count in ascitic fluid
→ Adults- By gram negative ! (E. coli, Klebsiella) or gram positive (S. hemolyticus)
- Mostly in preexisting ascites due to cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari snd, lupus, carcinomatosis
- Germ migration from
a) Intact bowels (transmural intestinal)
b) Blood stream in bacteriemia (hematogenous)
c) Infected fallopian tubes (direct ascending peritoneal contamination)
Gonococcal- Vulvo-vaginitis always precedes peritonitis
- Ascending trans-fallopian migration of vaginal and fallopian purulent secretion with
direct peritoneal contamination
- Clinical manifestations: violent, significant alteration of general condition
- Abdominal pus: abundant, green
- Bilateral purulent gonococcal salpingitis always associated
Tuberculous- Concomitant with an active focus of tuberculosis
- Contamination: hematogenous, lymphatic, trans-fallopian
- Sometimes even late after its apparent sterilization
Pneumococcal- Aggravates evolution of pat. with cirrhosis, alcoholics, HIV, Hep. C, during severe
pneumonia complicated with septicemia
→ Children
Pneumococcal
(Streptococcus pneumoniae)		- Severe complication in nephrotic syndrome, pneumococcal respiratory infections
(septicemia) or juvenile liver cirrhosis (bacterial trans-mural intestinal migration)
Hemolytic streptococcal- During scarlet fever or streptococcal tonsilitis

Clinical features

Children

  • Violent
  • Acute, intense, diffuse abdominal pain
  • Guarding, tenderness and rebound tenderness
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Ileus
  • High fever
  • Irritative diarrhea
  • same for adult females with gonococcal primary peritonitis

Adults

  • Tuberculous PP → onset is progressive, not acute; abdominal distension, nausea, moderate pain, usually without

guarding or tenderness; fever and typically night sweats

  • Liver cirrhosis → signs for peritoneal irritation might be absent; onset is gradual; mild fever 37.8-38 °C, metabolic

acidosis; ileus; sometimes hypothermia; most relevant - acute, apparently unexplained liver decompensation;

altered mental status

  • Some cases are totally asymptomatic !

Paracentesis and ascitic fluid examination

  • Leucocyte count: PMN > 250 cells/mm³
  • Bacterial culture (usually similar results with blood culture)
  • Protein concentration < 1g/dL
  • Glucose < 50 mg/dL
  • Lactate > 25mg/dL
  • pH < 7.35

Treatment

  • Non-surgical broad-spectrum AB
  • Has to be proven without any doubt → patients with secondary bacterial peritonitis eventually die under

conservative treatment, while patients with primary bacterial peritonitis + cirrhosis die after surgical treatment

  • Starting with empiric AB therapy (never wait for bacterial culture results !)
  • Usually with Claforan or Rocephine i.v. for 10-14 days
  • Clinic improvement should occur after 48 hours
  • Concomitant leukocyte decrease in ascitic fluid
  • AB therapy should be modified according to results of culture

DD to secondary peritonitis

  • Culture (primary = monobacterial; secondary = multibacterial with aerobic and anaerobic bac.)
  • X ray/ CT scan shows air = pneumoperitoneum in secondary PP

Secondary peritonitis (SP)

bacterial
Multi-microbial
  • Local vasodilatation → peritoneal (parietal and visceral) edema + constant plasma intra-peritoneal diffusion
  • fluid sequestration (third fluid compartment) → hypovolemic shock and kidney injury
  • Germs produce endo- and exotoxins → penetrate peritoneal membrane → systemic inflammatory response
  • Dynamic ileus additionally increases fluid sequestrations and aggravates cardio-pulmonary effects due to

important abdominal distension

  • Untreated → sepsis, septico-toxic shock with multiple organ failures and death
  • 1) Bacterial
    • Commonly from perforation of an intra-abdominal hollow viscera (aggressiveness of contaminating bacteria is

exponentially increasing from upper to lower segments of digestive tract → colon perforation is the worst

  • gram negative and anaerobic, exo- and endotoxins producing germs !)
  • Sometimes from abscesses located in intra-peritoneal, retro-peritoneal or pelvic parenchymatous organs (liver,

spleen, pancreas, kidneys, urinary bladder, uterus, ovaries)

a. Severe inflammation or ischemia → necroses, gangrenes → perforations

  • Perforated appendicitis - most common cause, usually causes only peri-appendicular abscess
  • Perforated duodenal ulcer - most typical picture with “wooden abdomen” and pneumoperitoneum in 70%
  • Perforated pyosalpinx – pelvic-peritonitis, well defined local signs, general good state
  • Perforated colic diverticulitis - rarely results in diffuse peritonitis; more frequently pericolic abscesses
  • Acute cholecystitis - rarely perforates into greater peritoneal cavity
  • Peritonitis with hepatic starting point caused by superinfected hepatic abscesses or cysts (very uncommon)
  • Bowel infarctions
  • Torsions
  • Internal strangulated hernias
  • Meckel’s diverticula
  • Malignant bowel perforations
  • Toxic mega-colon perforation
  • Fistulas

b. Abdominal traumatisms

  • Traumatic visceral ruptures/ perforations by blunt abdominal trauma
  • Stab wounds or gunshots (perforation of an organ might not be present)
  • Foreign-body-triggered digested tract perforations

c. Iatrogenic

  • After abdomino-pelvic surgeries or accidental perforations (e.g., ERCP)
  • Peritoneal catheter (adult patients with feeding jejunal tubes, juvenile patients with peritoneal dialysis)
  • 2) Chemical
    • Contaminant initially sterile
    • Classically biliary peritonitis due to gangrenous (ischemic) necrosis of gallbladder or due to biliragia (duodenal

perforation, CBD perforation, liver injury)

  • Acute pancreatitis with parenchymal necrosis (pancreatic enzymes)
  • First hours after gastric perforation (hydrochloric acid)

DD

  • Acute abdomen BUT becauses surgery is indicated in any secondary PP, less important
  • False medical acute abdomen
  • MI (→ EKG)
  • Basal pneumonia, pericarditis, pleuritis (auscultation, X-ray)
  • Lower chest neuromyalgias (history of erythematous lesions, X-rays)
  • Type 1 and 5 hyperlipidemia (epigastric pain)
  • Advanced RF and decompensated DM (intense abdominal pain)
  • Typhoid fever
  • Acute arsenic poisoning
  • Food poisoning

Medical acute abdomen includes

  • Biliary colic
  • Renal colic
  • Tabetic gastric crisis
  • Chronic lead exposure (specific gingival line)
  • Acute intermittent porphyria → DD Watson-Schwartz test and on change in color of urine exposed to light

Diagnosis

  • General appearance → deeply suffering person, anxious look, sunken eyes immobile
  • Even slightest movement (deep breathing, sneezing, coughing) generates pain
  • Nausea common; hiccough and vomiting are very painful
  • Abdominal pain has an abrupt onset, severe and continuous; initially localized but soon becomes diffuse
Inspection- Initially flat abdomen, completely immobile, shallow respiratory movements
- Later (after 6-8 hours) abdominal progressive distension develops
Palpation
(most
important)		- Causes very intense pain
- Diffuse abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness, guarding, rigidity
(classically described in peptic perforated ulcers as “wooden abdomen”)
- Positive Blumberg sign
- These clinical findings fade after 6-8 hours, due to abdominal muscle exhaustion,
rigidity diminishes and finally disappears → replaced by abdominal distension
- Abdominal cutaneous hyperestesia, abolishment of abdominal cutaneous reflexes
Percussion- Particularly painful (Bell sign and Grassmann-Mandel)
- Intense tympanism (liver dullness obliterated) especially in cases with hollow
organ perforation
- Concomitant presence of fluid (pus, bile, infected ascitis) revealed as dullness
Auscultation- No bowel sounds → “silentium abdominis”
DRE- Mandatory and reveals swollen and very painful Douglas pouch

Imaging

Abdominal X-ray- Useful when perforated peptic ulcer is suspected
- Shows classic “pneumoperitoneum”
Abdominal US- Reveals fluid in abdomen, distended bowels without peristaltic movements and
other specific elements concerning underlying cause (perforated lithiasic
gallbladder, perforated appendix, free air in hollow organ perforation)
CT- By far the best imaging technique, able not only to confirm diagnosis but also
underlying cause
Laparoscopy- Very useful procedure, diagnostic and therapeutic

* NEVER do endoscopy (pumps even more air into the peritoneum

Treatment

= surgical emergency → even with correct treatment, high mortality

  • 1. Preoperative preparation
  • Concomitant with blood-tests and EKG
  • Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Pain control after positive diagnosis has been established (opioids)
  • Prompt and efficient re-hydration (large venous catheters)
  • Naso-gastric suction tube to obtain gastric vacuity !!!
  • Oxygen per mask
  • Urinary catheter
  • 2. Surgery
  • Has three main goals (treatment principles by Kirschner)
I. Control contaminating source
- Removal of affected organ (appendix, gallbladder)
- Resection of organ or perforated segment (stomach, enterectomy, colon)
- Limited resection of affected area and suture (duodenal ulcer)
- Plain suture or suture and omentoplasty of perforation
- Externalization of perforated segment with restoration of digestive continuity in 2nd stage
(e.g. Hartman’s surgery)
- Lavage of peritoneal cavity
II. Eliminate septic abdominal content
- Pus, feces, bile, urine, digestive tract content removed by thorough and abundant peritoneal lavage
- Washing with many litters of warm saline fluid
→ Attention in several narrow spaces (left and right sub-phrenic spaces, Douglas pouch, spaces
between bowel loops)
- Good, efficient peritoneal lavage prevents early and late postoperative adhesions and developing of
residual intra-abdominal abscesses
III. Drain peritoneal cavity
- Multiple abdominal drainages placed in narrow spaces to prevent abscesses
- All tubes are exteriorized through abdominal wall and removed after 48-72 hours
  • Procedures done laparoscopically
  • In long-standing, neglected peritonitis with intraabdominal adhesions → large xypho-pubic median laparotomy
  • First maneuver after entering into abdominal cavity, is to obtain a sample of pus (or whatever contaminating agent)

for bacterial culture

Prognosis

  • Gold time period (first 6 h) are very important, later mortality rapidly increases !

Acute localized peritonitis

= inflammatory process, purulent collections, localized in part of peritoneal cavity

  • Occurs due to blocking of appendix, gallbladder or duodenal ulcer perforation by greater omentum
  • Intraperitoneal abscesses occur secondarily to generalized peritonitis
  • Depending on location, abscesses can be
Subphrenic- Also termed supramesocolic are supra- and subhepatic
Suprahepatic- Right and left inter-hepato-diaphragmatic and intersplenophrenic
SubmesocolicSubmesocolic- Interileal, perisigmoid, right and left parieto-colic, left mesenterico-colic, subcecal and
periappendicular

Clinically

  • Guarding with general infection signs
  • Fever, tachycardia
  • Suppressed transit, irritation diarrhea being quite frequently found
  • Hyperleukocytosis with neutrophilia (proportional to infection)
  • Interhepato-diaphragmatic abscesses occur after biliary and liver surgery (hydatid cyst, hepatectomy)
  • Clinical exam: lower respiratory amplitude, lower inferior liver margin, possibly basal pleural collection
  • Radiological exam: high hemidiaphragm, pneumoperitoneum
  • Replaced by US (additionally allows assess the content, walls and volume of abscess)

Tertiary peritonitis (TP)

  • Usually develops in patients with severe comorbidities or immunocompromised (e.g. AIDS/HIV, diabetic, advanced

neoplasias, aged, malnourished, hypoalbuminemic, anemic, cirrhotic)

  • Represent intra-peritoneal infections that persist or recur 48 hours after initially efficient surgical and antibiotic

treatment

Aggravating factors

  • Multi-resistant nosocomial bacteria
  • Enterococci, Enterobacter and fungi
  • Diagnosis is not simple → re-laparatomy
  • Earlier diagnosis by repeatedly followed values of C-reactive protein
  • If strong suspicions raised, early re-laparatomy with peritoneal lavage and abdominal fluid culture mandatory

book.html:
Peritonitis

Doru Munteanu

Anatomy:The anatomical boundaries of the abdominal cavity are represented cranially by the diaphragm, dorsally by the posterior abdominal wall (the spine and the Quadratus lombus muscles), ventrally and laterally by the antero-lateral abdominal muscles (Rectus abdominis, the oblique – external and internal – and the Transversus abdominis muscles respectively), together with their conjoined fascias and aponevroses; caudally, the abdominal cavity is delimited by the “diaphragm of the pelvis“(Levator ani and coccigeus muscles respectively). Between the diaphragmatic dome and the superior aperture of the pelvis the cavity is named “abdomen proper”, while the one between the superior aperture and the Levator ani muscle, is named pelvis.

The peritoneal cavity is contained into the abdominal one. It is a closed sack wrapped in thinmembrane (named peritoneum), which covers the internal surfaces of the above-mentioned musculo-fascial abdominal boundaries (parietal peritoneum); the posterior parietal peritoneum reflects anterior and wraps most of the abdominal organs (the intraperitoneal organs, the transverse mesocolon and mesentery) and becomes “the visceral peritoneum”); the intraperitoneal organs are: stomach, liver, gallbladder, first part of the duodenum, pancreas (only the tail), spleen, small bowel, appendix, transvers colon, sigmoid colon; they are contained into the intraperitoneal space.

The retroperitoneal space is situated behind the peritoneal cavity, between the posterior parietal peritoneum and the posterior muscular wall of the abdominal cavity and containes the retroperitoneal organs (esophagus, aorta, vena cava, duodenum, pancreas - head and body - , bladder, ureters, kidneys, adrenal glands, ascending and descending colon).

With an unfolded surface area of 1.5-2m², peritoneum is the largest serous membrane in the human body; being a well vascularized mesothelial membrane it has dialyzing properties, thus allowing for fluids, germs, toxins and small molecules to pass.

Definition:inflammation (vascular congestion, edema) of the visceral and parietal peritoneum, triggered by a local, regional or general pathology.

Classification I.:- Diffuse peritonitis (generalized)

  • Abdominal abscesses (localized).

Classification II. :● Primary

  • Secondary
  • Tertiary.

● Primary peritonitis (PP):

  • - Etio-pathogenyPrimary peritonitis are also known as spontaneous

bacterial peritonitis)(SBP) and have two main characteristics: - most of the cases are monomicrobial (>90%), and a.

  • low level of proteins and leucocytes count in the ascitic fluid.

a - In adults: - PP are most frequently caused by the contamination with gram-negative (E coli or Klebsiella), or gram–positive germs (S. pneumoniae, S. haemolyticus), of preexisting ascitic fluid (of any type), especially in cases with decompensated cirrhoses, Budd-Chiari syndrome, lupus erythematosus, disseminated malignancies. The pathogenic mechanisms consist of germs’migration from intact bowels (trans-mural-intestinal), from the blood stream (hematogenous) during episodes of bacteriemia, or from the infected fallopian tubes (direct ascending peritoneal contamination). Although E. coli and K. pneumoniae are responsible for almost 50% of all PP, a number of other particular etio-pathogenic types of PP have been described:

  • Gonococcal primary peritonitis: In these cases, vulvo-vaginitis always

precedes the peritonitis; the mechanism of contamination consists of ascending trans-fallopian migration of the vaginal and fallopian purulent secretion with direct peritoneal contamination; clinical manifestations of peritonitis are violent, with significant alteration off patients’ general condition; abdominal pus is abundant, green; bilateral purulent gonococcal salpingitis is always associated.

  • Tuberculous primary peritonitis:may occur concomitant with an active

focar of tuberculosis (contamination may be hematogenous, lymphatic-from positive abdominal lymph nodes-, or trans-fallopian), sometimes even late after its apparent sterilization.

  • Pneumococcal primary peritonitis – aggravates the evolution of patients

with liver cirrhosis, alcoholics, HIV infection or C-virus chronic hepatitis, during a severe episode of pneumonia complicated with septicaemia (hematogenous contamination of the ascetic fluid in patients with an inefficient immune defense).

b - In children: - Pneumococcal (Streptococcus pneumoniae) primary peritonitis: ascending trans-fallopian migration of the germs from an infected vagina is a rare mechanism these days. More frequently, it represents today a severe complication in children with nephrotic syndrome, pneumococcal respiratory infections (septicaemia) or juvenile liver cirrhosis (bacterial trans-mural intestinal migration).

  • Haemolitic streptococcal primary peritonitis: - occurs during scarlet

fever or streptococcal tonsilitis.

- Diagnosis:

The clinical features ofprimary peritonitis are different in juvenile patients from adult ones●in children, clinical manifestations are violent, with acute and intense, diffuse abdominal pain, abdominal guarding, tenderness and rebound tenderness, nausea and vomiting, bowel paresis, high fever and irritative diarrhoea; the same goes for adult females with gonococcal primary peritonitis. On the other hand, in adult patients with●tuberculous primary peritonitis, the onset is progressive, not acute, with abdominal distension, nausea, moderate pain, usually without guarding or tenderness, but with fever and typically, night sweats. ●Particularly, in patients with liver cirrhosis, sometimes the signs for peritoneal irritation are absent, the onset is gradual, with body temperature 37.8-38C, metabolic acidosis, bowel paresis, sometimes hypothermia; most relevant in these cases is the acute, apparently unexplained liver decompensation, altered mental status. Some cases are totally asymptomatic!

Paracentesis and ascitic fluid examination:- leucocytes count: - PMN >250 cells/mm³

  • bed-side bacterial culture from the ascitic fluid (usually similar results

with the blood culture)

  • protein concentration < 1g/dL.
  • glucose < 50 mg/dL
  • lactate > 25mg/dL
  • pH < 7.35.

-Treatment:

Nonsurgical broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment is the indication of choice in these cases. We must emphasise that the accuracy of the diagnosis has to be beyond any doubt, as all patients with secondary microbial peritonitis treated conservatively (with antibiotics but without surgery) will die, while mortality rates in cirrhotic decompensated cases with primary bacterial peritonitis will exceed 80% after surgical treatment! Thus, in cases with proven positive diagnosis of PP, starting with an empiric antibiotherapy is the best option (never wait for the fluid bacterial cultures’ results!), usually with Claforan,( i.v., 3x2g/day), or Rocephine, (i.v., 2x1g/day) for 10-14 days. Clinic improvement should occur after 48 hours. Concomitant decrease in the leucocytes count of ascitic fluid is another indicator of treatment efficacy. Antibiotherapy should be modified according to the results of the culture.

● Secondary peritonitis (SP):

  • - Etio-pathogeny – InSP the most common source of peritoneal

inflammation is an acute bacterial infection (bacterial peritonitis); the origin of the pathogens is, in the vast majority of the cases, the intra-abdominal hollow viscera, among which, perforated acute appendicitis and perforated duodenal peptic ulcers are classically the most frequent ones. However, we emphasize that the intra-peritoneal spillage of every single hollow organ’s content can contaminate the peritoneal cavity due to severe inflammation or ischaemia, with consequent necroses, gangrenes, or perforations (bowel infarctions, torsions, internal strangulated hernias, perforated colon diverticulitis, peri-appendicular abscess, Meckel’s diverticula, malignant bowel perforations, toxic mega-colon perforation, foreign-body-triggered digested tract perforations, etc). Abdominal traumatisms (traumatic visceral ruptures/perforations caused by blunt abdominal traumas, stab wounds or gunshots) are possible machanisms as well. A special category of peritonitis is represented by the so-called chemical peritonitis: in these cases, the contaminant is, at least initially, sterile. The classic example is a rare type of biliary peritonitis, namely the so-called “peritonitis sine perforation”; it happens during gangrenous (ischaemic) necrosis of the gallbladder (in diabetic or septic patients). In these cases, paradoxically, although there is no evident perforation, the bile fluid is filtered-out through the microscopically compromised gallbladder walls, in the peritoneal cavity; acute pancreatitis (initially, the irritating abdominal fluid is rich in pancreatic enzymes, but sterile), or in the first hours after a gastric perforation (the spilled acid gastric content is in the initial phases sterile, but generates an important peritoneal irritation/inflammation). Apart from the intra-peritoneal hollow organs, abscesses or necroses located in the intra-peritoneal, retro-peritoneal or pelvic parenchymatous organs (liver, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, urinary bladder, uterus, ovaries), can generate peritonitis as well.

It is worth to be emphasized that the aggressiveness of the contaminating bacteria is exponentially increasing from the upper to the distal segments of the digestive tract (e.g. gastric perforations are initially sterile, while colonic perforations generate peritonitis with severe prognosis, due to a “heavy load” of Gram-negative and anaerobic, exo-and endotoxines-producing germs !).

External (extra-abdominal) peritoneal contamination may result as well in acute peritonitis, whether via an open abdominal trauma (penetrating abdominal wounds with no visceral involvement), an ascending transfallopian migration of germs-direct contamination-(gonococcal peritonitis), or a peritoneal catheter (adult patients with feeding jejunal tubes, juvenile patients with peritoneal dialysis).

Secondary peritonites are multi-microbial, anaerobic germs coexisting with the aerobic ones. Once the peritoneal membrane has been contaminated, the local defence mechanisms are activated (complement), with production of macrophages and cytokines and concomitant migration of granulocytes intra-peritoneally. Due to its large surface area (1.5-2 m²), the local important vasodilatation, the peritoneal (parietal and visceral as well) edema, together with a constant plasma intra-peritoneal diffusion, an importantloco-regional fluids sequestration occurs, creating a third parasitic fluids’ compartment with consecutive hypovolaemic shock.Germs, together with their endo-and exotoxines, will penetrate through the peritoneal membrane and generate the systemic inflammatory response. The increased cardiac output demanded together with the combined toxic systemic effects of the causative germs will have dramatic effects especially on elderly patients. Another important locoregional consequence, is the bowel paresis; it supplementary increases the fluid sequestrations and aggravates the cardio-pulmonary effects due to the important abdominal distension. If untreated, SP will generate sepsis, septico-toxic shock with multiple organ failures and death, within days (in up to 20-40% of the cases).

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical features: - General appearance is that of a deeply suffering

person, with an anxious look, sunken eyes immobile. The patient lies still, rigid, immobile, with thighs flexed in order to relief abdominal tension. Even the slightest movement (deep breathing, sneezing, coughing) generates pain. Nausea is common; hiccough and vomiting are very painful.

  • Abdominal painhas an abrupt onset, is severe and continuous; initially

it always is localized but soon becomes diffuse.

  • Inspection: initially, the abdomen is flat, completely immobile, patient

having shallow respiratory movements (thoracic-type only). Later on, after 6-8 hours, abdominal progressive distension develops.

  • Auscultation: reveals no bowel sounds, as peristaltic movements are

abolished (bowel paresis) (“silentium abdominis”).

  • Percussion is particularly painful (bell-sign – Grassmann-Mandel),

revealing several hours after onset, intense tympanism (liver dullness obliterated) especially in cases with hollow organs’ perforations. The concomitant presence of fluid (pus, bile infected ascitis, etc) is revealed as dullness.

  • Palpation: - is a particularly important maneuver; in these cases still, it

has to be done very gently, mild, as it causes very intense pain. The patient presents diffuse abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness,guarding, and rigidity (classically described in cases of peptic perforated ulcersas “wooden abdomen”). Sudden retraction of the palpating hand will cause, typically, pain (Blumberg sign). In time, though, the “quality” of these clinical findings fade, as after 6-8 hours, due to the abdominal muscles’ exhaustion, the rigidity diminishes and finally disappears to be replaced by the abdominal distension. Abdominal cutaneous hyperestesia, and abolishment of the abdominal cutaneous reflexes are present as well.

We here draw the attention on this particularly important clinical aspect, as the most severely altered patients, with long standing peritonites (12-24 hours or more), may present with poor and tricky, completely altered clinical signs and symptoms (pain has lost most of its intensity, abdominal rigidity has disappeared, guarding has diminished, the flat and rigid abdomen has been replaced by an enormously distended one).

  • Rectal examination: is mandatory and reveals a swelled-up and very

painful Douglas’ pouch.

Imaging diagnosis

1. Abdominal X-ray examination is useful when a perforated peptic ulcer is suspected; it shows the classic “pneumoperitoneum” , i.e., the presence of free air under the diaphragm.

2.Abdominal ultrasonography - reveales the fluid into the abdomen, distended bowels without peristaltic movements and other specific elements concerning the underlying cause of the peritonitis (perforated lithiasic gallbladder, a perforated appendix, free air into the abdominal cavity – signifying the perforation of a hollow viscus - ), etc.

3.CT scan is by far the best imaging technique, able not only to confirm the diagnosis of peritonitis, but, in a significant number of cases, it accurately detects the underlying cause.

4. Laparoscopy is a very useful procedure, as once the diagnostic phase has been successfully accomplished, the therapeutic phase may follow (in recent peritonites, virtually all the underlying causes can be treated by a laparoscopic approach).

We emphasize here another important aspect, namely, that, ones the positive diagnosis of acute abdomen, caused by secondary peritonitis, has been established, the specific and detailedcause is not any more relevant, as long as the indication for surgery has been established.

Treatment:

SP represents a surgical emergency and in spite of competent treatment still has significant mortality rates.

Once the diagnosis has been established, a competent resuscitation of the patient starts as part of the brief preoperative preparation:

-Concomitant with the blood-tests and EKG,

-Antibiotherapy is started with an empiric formula of broad-spectrum antibiotics;

-Pain has to be controlled, once the positive diagnosis has been established

-Prompt and efficient rehydration (large venou catheters)

-Naso-gastric suction tube – in order to obtain gastric vacuity

-Urinary catheter.

Surgery:has three main goals: I- to control the contaminating source;

II- to eliminate the septic abdominal content (pus, feces, bile, urine, digestive tract content, etc) by a thorough and abundant peritoneal lavage;

III- to drain the peritoneal cavity.

I. Controlling the contaminating source is accomplished depending on the underlying cause (e.g., appendectomy, cholecystectomy, Meckel’s diverticulectomy, enterectomy for perforated strangulated/necrotized bowels, suture of a perforated peptic ulcer, etc).

II. Abundant washing of the peritoneal cavity must be done careful and in detail, in order to completely remove the contaminating agent; it takes many litters of warm saline fluid; care must be taken in several narrow spaces of the abdominal cavity, where the washing maneuvers have to be especially thorough (left and right sub-phrenic spaces, Douglas’ pouch, the spaces between the bowel loops), as no remnant contaminating agent can be left behind. A good, efficient peritoneal lavage, prevents early and late postoperative adhesions, but more important, prevents developing of residual intra-abdominal abscesses, a complication that can compromise the entire procedure and the patient’s prognosis!

III. After the first two phases, multiple abdominal drainages are placed, namely in the above-mentioned “Narrow spaces” with higher risk for developing residual abscesses: the both left and right subphrenic spaces, the “Bursa omentalis” (this so-called sub-hepatic drain tube is introduced with the internal extremity, through the Hiatus of Winslow, into the retro-gastric “Bursa omentalis”, thus preventing a residual retro-gastric abscess; the last drain-tube is placed in the Douglas’ pouch; all tubes are exteriorized through the abdominal wall and will be removed the next 48-72 hours.

All the above-mentioned maneuvers can be done laparoscopically.

In cases with long-standing, neglected peritonites, where intraabdominal adhesions are expected to have been developed, in order to an efficient peritoneal lavage and drainage, a large xypho-pubic median laparotomy is required.

We emphasize that the first maneuver after entering into the abdominal cavity, is to obtain a sample of pus (or whatever the contaminating agent is) for bacterial culture.

  • Tertiary peritonitis (TP):

TP develop usually in patients with severe comorbidities or immunocompromised (i.e.,AIDS/HIV, diabetic, advanced neoplasias, aged, malnourished, hypoalbuminaemic, anaemic, cirrhotic,etc) and represent intra-peritonealinfections that persist or recur 48 hours after an initially efficient surgical and antibiotic treatment. The aggravating particularities of this particular type of peritonitis are: - the bacteria involved here are most frequently the most feard ones, namely the multi-resistant nosocomial ones (Enterococi, Enterobacter) and fungi as well. Diagnosis is not simple, thus on demand or planned relaparatomy have been proposed. Yet earlier diagnosis can be established by using, among other criteria, the repeatedly followed values of C-reactive protein.

If strong enough suspicions are raised, early relaparatomy with peritoneal lavage and abdominal fluid culture is mandatory.
